inputs.need:
I am the associate program director for assessment in a 90-resident internal medicine residency. Residents receive workplace-based assessments (mini clinical evaluation exercises and case-based discussions) on a web form, and each form has one free-text feedback box. When our competence committee reviewed 200 forms from last year, most comments were generic, such as "good job" or "keep reading", and only about one in four said what the resident did, what to change and how. Residents tell us the comments are not useful, and the committee struggles to make progress decisions from them.

We want to run a quality improvement project using PDSA cycles to raise the proportion of forms with actionable written feedback. Change ideas we are considering: relabelling and then splitting the free-text box into two prompts ("one thing to keep doing" and "one thing to do differently next time"), a 20-minute micro-teaching session at faculty meetings, and a monthly report to each faculty member showing their own comments rated against a short checklist. We would rate a weekly sample of comments against three criteria (specific behaviour, clear gap, concrete next step) and show the results on a run chart.

I need help with the aim statement, the operational definition of an actionable comment, the balancing measures (for example fewer forms completed, or forms completed later), and how to avoid bias when we rate the comments. We also worry that comment quality differs by resident gender, so we want to look at that. We have no funding; the chief residents can rate forms, and faculty meetings happen monthly. We would like to start in October and run until March.
inputs.constraints: No funding. Rating is done by the two chief residents in two hours of protected time a week. The software administrator can relabel the existing feedback field now but cannot add a second field before January 2027. Faculty meetings are monthly and can give 20 minutes to the project.

The program director approved 20 minutes at each monthly faculty meeting from October 2026 to March 2027 (approval PD-2026-08, dated 2026-08-18).
Last year 2,340 workplace-based assessment forms were completed, about 45 a week; the committee found actionable comments on 52 of 200 sampled forms.
The two chief residents have two hours a week of protected time for education projects.

records.title: Rating the quality of narrative comments on workplace-based assessment forms: development of a three-criterion checklist
records.authors: Lindahl-Osei M, Fairbanks-Ruiz T, Chaudhry-Welsh A
records.abstract: We developed a checklist for rating written comments on workplace-based assessment forms. Three criteria were retained after two rounds of expert review: the comment names a specific observed behaviour, identifies a gap between performance and the expected standard, and proposes a concrete next step. Two trained raters applied the checklist to 600 comments from three internal medicine programmes. Agreement was substantial (kappa 0.74), and rating took about 40 seconds per comment. Only 35 percent of comments met all three criteria, and generic praise was the most common comment type. The checklist is intended for monitoring feedback quality, not for judging individual faculty.

records.title: Prompted feedback fields on assessment forms and the specificity of written comments: a before-after study
records.abstract: One residency programme replaced a single free-text box on its workplace-based assessment form with two prompts: one thing to keep doing and one thing to do differently. We rated 400 comments from the six months before and 400 from the six months after the change with a three-criterion checklist. The proportion of comments meeting all three criteria rose from 31 to 52 percent. Median comment length rose from 14 to 29 words, and the number of forms completed per month did not change. Raters were not blinded to the period, which may have inflated the difference.

records.title: Brief faculty workshops on feedback and the quality of written comments: a controlled before-after study across two programmes
records.authors: Kaczmarek-Bello J, Thorne-Adeyemi C, Vasquez-Lund R
records.abstract: Faculty in one internal medicine programme attended two 20-minute workshops on written feedback, while a second programme continued as usual. Comments were rated blind to programme and period. At three months, the proportion of actionable comments rose by 14 percentage points in the workshop programme compared with 2 points in the comparison programme. By six months, without reminders, the difference had narrowed to 5 points. Attendance was 68 percent, and faculty who attended both sessions improved most. The authors conclude that brief teaching helps but fades without reinforcement.

records.title: Resident perceptions of useful written feedback: a multi-site study of 540 trainees
records.abstract: We asked 540 residents in eight programmes to rate 30 real comments, stripped of identifiers, for usefulness. Comments that named a next step were rated most useful, and generic praise was rated least useful even when residents said they valued encouragement. Residents rated a comment's usefulness similarly whether it came from a senior or a junior faculty member. More than half said they rarely read the free-text comments on their forms because they expected them to be generic. The authors recommend that programmes monitor the specificity of comments rather than their number.

records.title: Gendered language in narrative assessment comments for internal medicine residents
records.authors: Abernathy-Mensah L, Rios-Kowalczyk D, Sorensen-Uba P
records.abstract: We analysed 3,100 narrative comments written for internal medicine residents in three programmes. Comments about women residents were more likely to describe personal attributes such as being pleasant or hardworking, and comments about men were more likely to describe clinical reasoning. After adjustment for postgraduate year and rotation, women were 1.4 times as likely as men to receive a comment with no actionable content. Differences were largest in comments written by faculty who completed the fewest forms. The authors recommend reporting feedback quality by resident gender whenever it is monitored.

records.title: Monthly individual feedback reports to faculty on their assessment comments: a run-chart evaluation
records.abstract: A programme sent each faculty member a monthly one-page report showing a sample of their own written comments rated against a three-criterion checklist, with the programme median for comparison. Over 14 months, the monthly median proportion of actionable comments rose from 28 to 47 percent, with a shift on the run chart from month five. Faculty who opened the report email more than half the time improved most. The number of forms completed per resident did not fall. There was no comparison group, and a new assessment policy was introduced during month nine.

records.title: Time from encounter to form completion and the specificity of written feedback
records.abstract: We examined 1,800 workplace-based assessment forms and the delay between the observed encounter and the completion of the form. Comments on forms completed within 24 hours were more specific than those completed after 48 hours: 41 percent against 19 percent met all three quality criteria. Forms completed late were more often completed in batches at the end of a rotation. Programme size and rotation type did not explain the difference. The authors suggest that prompting completion soon after the encounter may improve comment quality more than lengthening the form.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A three-criterion checklist rates comments reliably and quickly. Prompted fields, brief faculty teaching and monthly individual reports were each followed by more actionable comments, but only the teaching study had a comparison group and its effect faded without reminders. Forms completed late carry less specific comments, residents value comments with a next step, and women residents receive non-actionable comments more often. The evidence supports testing a combined package locally with a run chart, balancing measures and a gender breakdown rather than assuming an effect size.
response.gradeRationale: Mostly uncontrolled single-programme reports with one controlled before-after study; consistent direction but serious risk of bias and fading effects.

response.reading: Comment quality is shaped at three points: the form (what it asks for), the assessor (what they know and whether anyone shows them their own comments) and the moment of writing (soon after the encounter or in an end-of-rotation batch). The retrieved evidence supports changes at each point, with the strongest caution that teaching alone fades (claim c3) and that equity must be watched because women residents receive vaguer comments (claim c4). The committee and the residents are the users of the comments; the chief residents are the measurement system.

response.overview: Program-level QI project using the Model for Improvement: eight weekly baseline points rated from August and September 2026 forms, then three PDSA cycles from October 2026 to March 2027, with a weekly run chart of actionable comments.
response.population: All mini clinical evaluation exercise and case-based discussion forms completed for the 90 residents; each week 25 comments are sampled by form number from the week's completed forms.
response.exposure: Cycle 1 (October to December): feedback field relabelled 'What did the resident do well, and what should they do differently next time?' plus 20-minute micro-teaching in October and November. Cycle 2 (January to February): two separate fields, 'one thing to keep doing' and 'one thing to do differently next time'. Cycle 3 (February to March): a monthly one-page report to each faculty member with a sample of their own rated comments and the program median.
response.procedures: An administrator extracts comment text without dates, form layout or names and mixes baseline and current comments in each rating batch. Chief residents rate each comment against the three criteria using written definitions and examples; 20 percent are rated by both. Cycle decisions are made at the monthly faculty meeting from the run chart.

response.designSummary: Time-ordered weekly measurement on a run chart with pre-specified rules; p-chart as a secondary display.
response.sampleSize: Twenty-five comments a week is what two chief residents can rate with double rating inside their protected time. With a baseline near 26 percent, a subgroup of 25 gives 3-sigma p-chart limits of about 26 points either side of the centre line, too wide to flag single weeks, so the run chart rules carry the judgement. A sustained rise to about 45 percent would produce a shift of six or more consecutive points above the baseline median within the second cycle; the 24 intervention weeks allow the shift rule to trigger and the monthly gender breakdown to accumulate about 50 comments per group per month.
response.primaryAnalysis: Run chart of the weekly proportion with the baseline median as centre line; shift (six or more points on one side), trend (five or more in one direction), runs and an astronomical point agreed in advance. The median is frozen after baseline and re-estimated only after a sustained shift.
response.secondaryAnalysis: p-chart for context; monthly proportions by resident gender with 95 percent intervals; run charts for forms completed and days to completion; inter-rater agreement (kappa) each month.
response.missingData: Weeks with fewer than 25 forms are plotted with their actual subgroup size and annotated; comments that cannot be rated are counted and reported.

store.title: Actionable written feedback on workplace-based assessments in an internal medicine residency
store.problem.rawNeed:
I am the associate program director for assessment in a 90-resident internal medicine residency. Residents receive workplace-based assessments (mini clinical evaluation exercises and case-based discussions) on a web form, and each form has one free-text feedback box. When our competence committee reviewed 200 forms from last year, most comments were generic, such as "good job" or "keep reading", and only about one in four said what the resident did, what to change and how. Residents tell us the comments are not useful, and the committee struggles to make progress decisions from them.

We want to run a quality improvement project using PDSA cycles to raise the proportion of forms with actionable written feedback. Change ideas we are considering: relabelling and then splitting the free-text box into two prompts ("one thing to keep doing" and "one thing to do differently next time"), a 20-minute micro-teaching session at faculty meetings, and a monthly report to each faculty member showing their own comments rated against a short checklist. We would rate a weekly sample of comments against three criteria (specific behaviour, clear gap, concrete next step) and show the results on a run chart.

I need help with the aim statement, the operational definition of an actionable comment, the balancing measures (for example fewer forms completed, or forms completed later), and how to avoid bias when we rate the comments. We also worry that comment quality differs by resident gender, so we want to look at that. We have no funding; the chief residents can rate forms, and faculty meetings happen monthly. We would like to start in October and run until March.
